import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Pollock's (tetrahedral numbers) conjecture

Every positive integer is the sum of at most 5 tetrahedral numbers.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollock%27s_conjectures)
- [A797](https://oeis.org/A797)
- L. E. Dickson, *History of the Theory of Numbers, Vol. II: Diophantine Analysis*, Dover (2005), pp. 22–23
- Frederick Pollock, *On the extension of the principle of Fermat's theorem on the polygonal numbers to the higher order of series whose ultimate differences are constant*, Abstracts of the Papers Communicated to the Royal Society of London **5** (1850), 922–924
- H. E. Salzer and N. Levine, *Table of integers not exceeding 100000 that are not expressible as the sum of four tetrahedral numbers*, Math. Comp. **12** (1958), 141–144
- [MathWorld: Pollock's Conjecture](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/PollocksConjecture.html)
-/

namespace PollocksConjecture

open scoped BigOperators

/-  ## Definitions -/

/-- The $n$-th tetrahedral number: $T_n = \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{6}$. -/
def tetrahedral (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  n * (n + 1) * (n + 2) / 6

/-  ## Auxiliary definition -/

/-- The set of natural numbers that are **not** a sum of $4$ tetrahedral numbers. -/
def NotSumOfFourTetrahedral : Set ℕ :=
  {N : ℕ | ∀ f : Fin 4 → ℕ, N ≠ ∑ i, tetrahedral (f i)}

/-  ## Statements -/

/--
Pollock's (tetrahedral numbers) conjecture:
every integer is the sum of at most $5$ tetrahedral numbers.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem pollock_tetrahedral (N : ℕ) :
    ∃ f : Fin 5 → ℕ, N = ∑ i, tetrahedral (f i) := by
  sorry

/--
Salzer–Levine strengthening (as stated on Wikipedia/OEIS):
there are exactly $241$ integers that are not a sum of $4$ tetrahedral numbers, and the largest is $343867$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem pollock_tetrahedral.salzer_levine :
    IsGreatest NotSumOfFourTetrahedral 343867 := by
  sorry

/-- As stated on Wikipedia/OEIS (A797), the set of exceptions has cardinality $241$. -/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem pollock_tetrahedral.ncard_exceptions :
    type_of% pollock_tetrahedral.salzer_levine ↔
    NotSumOfFourTetrahedral.ncard = 241 := by
  sorry

end PollocksConjecture

findings.description: The Salzer–Levine reference in the module docstring (line 29) gives the title as “Table of integers not exceeding 100000 ...”. The actual title has 1000000. This is a bibliographic bound typo; the Lean statements and their constants are unaffected.
findings.source_evidence: Salzer and Levine, Math. Comp. 12 (1958), pp. 141–144, title: “Table of Integers Not Exceeding 1000000 That Are Not Expressible as the Sum of Four Tetrahedral Numbers”. Confirmed in the archived paper, https://archive.org/download/sim_mathematics-of-computation_1958-04_12_62/sim_mathematics-of-computation_1958-04_12_62_djvu.txt, and the publisher's Crossref record, https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1090/S0025-5718-1958-0099756-3.
findings.suggested_fix: Change 100000 to 1000000 in the bibliographic title on line 29.

reformulations.difference: Lean quantifies over all natural numbers, including zero, and uses exactly five summand positions with natural-number indices. Wikipedia states that every positive integer is a sum of at most five tetrahedral numbers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: tetrahedral 0 = 0. Any representation with at most five positive-index tetrahedral numbers can be padded with zero-index terms to obtain five positions; conversely, deleting zero-index terms leaves at most five positive-index terms. The additional N = 0 instance holds using five zeros. An independent Lean proof of the full equivalence with positive integers and lists of at most five positive indices compiled in /workspace/review/positive_equivalences.lean without using the sorry-backed conjectures.

reformulations.difference: Lean asserts only that 343867 is the greatest four-term exception, rather than explicitly conjoining this with the assertion that there are exactly 241 exceptions.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Let S be NotSumOfFourTetrahedral and E = S ∩ {n | n ≤ 343867}. The published table and independent finite computations establish that E has exactly 241 members and contains 343867. If 343867 is greatest in S, then S = E, giving cardinality 241. Conversely, S.ncard = 241 implies S is finite, since infinite sets have ncard 0. Since E ⊆ S and both have cardinality 241, S = E, so 343867 is greatest. Thus the maximum-only formulation is equivalent to the full strengthening and to its cardinality formulation. The general finite-data equivalence was proved in Lean; the specific enumeration was checked by Lean #eval and independently in C++, not incorporated into a complete Lean proof of the specific biconditional.

H. E. Salzer and N. Levine, original paper, pp. 141–144: https://archive.org/download/sim_mathematics-of-computation_1958-04_12_62/sim_mathematics-of-computation_1958-04_12_62_djvu.txt

review.notes: All two definitions and three theorems were checked. Wikipedia and MathWorld still record the tetrahedral conjecture and the proposed last exception as conjectural. The textbook ncard_exceptions declaration is a valid equivalence lemma, not a claim that the open cardinality conjecture has been solved; ncard's infinite-set default causes no defect because 241 is nonzero. Independent Lean proofs verified exact division by 6, the zero boundary, and that 17 requires five rather than four terms. Lean enumeration found 241 four-term exceptions through 343867, ending at 343867. Independent C++ enumeration through 1000000 matched every entry of the OEIS b-file and found no five-term exceptions. The OEIS main entry was blocked by HTTP 403, but its b-file was accessible; both original papers were read through Internet Archive copies. All experiments are in /workspace/review/; the reviewed file was not modified.
